title: Quadkey / Tile XYZ Helper: Point to Tiles
description: Bridge a coordinate to its tile XYZ and quadkey with the Quadkey / Tile XYZ Helper — Bing-style tile addressing from any lat/lng. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square at zoom 15 is tile (9649, 12314), quadkey 032010110132021 — one point addressed in both dialects of the tile world from a single paste.
quick_answer: The Quadkey / Tile XYZ Helper bridges a latitude/longitude point to the tiled web-map concepts many basemap systems use: its XYZ tile numbers and its Bing quadkey at any zoom. Enter the point and read both addresses — the helper for anyone moving between slippy-map tiles and quadkey-indexed data.
steps_intro: One point, two tile dialects — fluent in both:

body.t: Bing's tile system and quadkey-keyed datasets meet the XYZ world here. Dedicated converters —
and its reverse — handle strings you already hold.
A feature sits right in one stack and one tile off in another: compare the point's XYZ and quadkey and the translation bug confesses.
Seeing a point's numbers in both systems at several zooms teaches the pyramid faster than any diagram.
Imagery and statistics keyed by quadkey join to XYZ-keyed layers through the shared point — the helper is the Rosetta stone.

032010110132021 decodes digit by digit from the top of the pyramid: each digit (0–3) picks a quadrant — NW, NE, SW, SE in the quadkey convention — and the string's length IS the zoom (15 digits, zoom 15).
Drop the last digit and you hold the parent tile at zoom 14; drop four, the zoom-11 ancestor. Quadkeys make tile genealogy a string operation — the property databases love.

popular_table.title: Two dialects, one grid
popular_table.intro: XYZ and quadkey describe the same pyramid.
popular_table.note: A quadkey is the tile's x and y bits interleaved and read in base 4 — the conversion is pure arithmetic, no lookup tables, which is why the two converters on this site are exact.

faq: A tile's address written as one string: each digit narrows to a quadrant, zoom equals length. Bing Maps popularised it; tile-keyed databases adopted it.
Each level has four children. Two bits per level — one from x, one from y — make one base-4 digit.
Yes — the Web Mercator slippy pyramid. Quadkey and XYZ are two notations for identical tiles (modulo the TMS y-flip some stacks apply).
The zoom your data lives at — imagery and statistics are published per level. The helper shows the address at the zoom you ask for.
A region is a set of tiles; quadkey ranges and prefix sets describe it compactly — a list operation, seeded from corner tiles computed here.
A quadkey names a whole tile, not a point — at zoom 15 in New York, a ~926 m square. Finer zooms name smaller squares.
Entirely — '032...' and '32...' are different tiles at different zooms. Never store quadkeys as numbers; the zeros are load-bearing.
